hidden_target.material_initial_state: An as-cast, equimolar WTaTiVZr refractory high-entropy alloy made from >99.99% pure elemental powders; the comparison baseline was a commercially sourced, powder-sintered pure tungsten plate with coarse equiaxed grains (~100 ± 20 µm).
hidden_target.intervention: The WTaTiVZr alloy was synthesized by arc melting and remelted at least five times, then its phase constitution, microstructure, compressive behavior, temperature-dependent indentation response, and scratch-based fracture toughness were measured and compared with commercially used pure tungsten.
hidden_target.conditions: Room-temperature uniaxial compression used 4 mm × 4 mm cylindrical specimens at an engineering strain rate of 0.001 s^-1. Indentation plastometry used 5 mm cubes, a 1 mm-radius Si3N4 indenter, loads up to 5 kN, and temperatures from room temperature to 500 °C in 100 °C increments. Scratch testing used a 200 µm-radius Rockwell C diamond stylus under a constant 100 N normal load at 0.01 mm/s over 3 mm; tests were repeated at least three times.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: A solidification-segregated dendritic microstructure containing two BCC phases with slightly different lattice parameters: W-Ta-rich dendrites and Zr-Ti-rich interdendritic regions, with V distributed between both phases.
hidden_target.mechanism: The high strength was attributed to multicomponent solid-solution strengthening, lattice distortion, and frictional resistance associated particularly with W and Ta. Improved plasticity and damage tolerance were attributed to Ti, V, and Zr, potentially through reduced valence-electron concentration, dislocation-core modification, improved grain-boundary cohesion, localized plastic deformation, and impeded crack propagation; these mechanistic assignments were presented as interpretations rather than directly isolated causal measurements.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to commercially used pure tungsten, the as-cast WTaTiVZr alloy was expected to provide higher room- and high-temperature strength, greater plastic strain, a lower brittle-to-ductile transition temperature, less scratch-induced cracking and damage, and higher fracture toughness.
hidden_target.baseline: Commercially used powder-sintered pure tungsten: single-phase BCC, coarse equiaxed grains, indentation-derived yield strength of ~700 MPa at room temperature and ~250 MPa at 500 °C, negligible plasticity through 300 °C with ductile behavior emerging near 400 °C, and scratch-based fracture toughness of ~25 ± 1 MPa√m.
hidden_target.boundary: The reported mechanical advantage applies to the as-cast equimolar alloy under quasi-static compression, indentation plastometry from room temperature through 500 °C, and room-temperature scratch testing. The HEA remained relatively brittle at low temperature, showing ~6% room-temperature plastic strain, quasi-cleavage fracture, and radial indentation cracks from 25 to 200 °C; indentation cracking was absent above 200 °C. Irradiation performance and service behavior in an operating fusion environment were not tested.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: XRD, SEM/BSE, EDS, and reported EBSD characterized phases and segregation; uniaxial compression measured yield strength, ultimate compressive strength, and plastic strain; temperature-dependent indentation plastometry measured strength, plastic strain, and crack disappearance; confocal scratch-track profilometry and transverse-force measurements were used to calculate KC from groove perimeter and projected contact area, with SEM assessing cracking and chipping.
hidden_target.actual_result: The alloy contained major and minor BCC phases in W-Ta-rich dendrites and Zr-Ti-V-rich interdendritic regions. Bulk compression gave ~1.6 GPa yield strength, ~1.8 GPa ultimate compressive strength, and ~6% plastic strain at room temperature, followed by shear-dominated quasi-cleavage fracture. Indentation-derived yield strength decreased from ~1.66 GPa at room temperature to ~650 MPa at 500 °C, still more than 2.5 times tungsten's ~250 MPa, while HEA plastic strain rose to >20% at 500 °C. Indentation cracks disappeared above 200 °C for the HEA versus around 400 °C for tungsten. Scratch grooves in the HEA were shallower and more uniform with fewer cracks and less damage, and its KC was ~38 ± 1 MPa√m versus ~25 ± 1 MPa√m for tungsten, an increase of about 52%.
